ployment; there is no question about that at all. The question is whether my hon. friends opposite are going to be allowed to say to the unemployed and the people of this country who need relief: We will do nothing for you unless in addition to the money that is required parliament gives us all the powers of parliament. In other words, unemployment relief is made a mere incident to the demand which is being made by hon. gentlemen opposite for power, and unlimited power. The time they say is one of national crisis, but such times I would point out were lived through by Macdonald in the old days when he occupied the position of my right hon. friend, and such times were lived through by other Prime Ministers, and they did not have to ask for these extraordinary powers. The Prime Minister could only quote the war time as a time when such powers were delegated to the government, and I would remind him, if reminding is of any use, that even in war time there was a definite limit placed on every bill voting money for the purpose of carrying on the war, and as I am reminded, at that time a specific sum wlas voted every year.
My right hon. friend in an endeavour to special plead a little bit in the matter of a blank cheque trots out some statutes, and he says in effect: Here are some statutes which indicate that we have been given a blank cheque before. But he knows better than that. He knows that the Old Age Pensions Act is not on all fours with this measure, and it does not need a lawyer to draw the distinction between them. The Old Age Pensions Act is an act to appropriate from year to year, practically in perpetuity, a sum which is never exactly known but is always capable of assessment, a sum which was limited in the act to so much per person, and a sum which is granted only after a certificate has been forwarded that a certain expenditure has been made by the province. That has nothing to do with the proposal before us, which is that for the purpose of exercising unlimited power the government gets unlimited grants of money.
My right hon. friend also mentioned the Montreal harbour bridge, and his followers cheered lustily about that. I have the bill before me relating to the Montreal harbour bridge. That bill does not provide as the statute which is to follow this resolution does for the building of a wharf or some other structure down in Nova Scotia, and at the same time for the building of a grain elevator or the construction of a highway in British Columbia. It provides for the construction of one specific
work, and for that work alone, a definite work across the harbour of Montreal, a bridge, and it provides that the harbour commission is authorized to build it. The only comfort my right hon. friend can get out of that, if there is any comfort in it at all for him, is that he says the governor in council-that is inferentially, because it says His Majesty- is authorized to guarantee the bonds issued by the commission for that undertaking.
With no limitations.

But the limitation is in
the work itself. That is expressly specified, and every expenditure under the act is required to be approved by the governor in council before they guarantee the bonds, and as my hon. friend from Quebec East suggests, the money is owed by the harbour commission, and so far as I know the commission is a debtor which probably can pay, and I do not think there will be any difficulty about the government collecting the money or any danger of its being called on under its guarantee. So that instance also goes by the board.
My right hon. friend quoted one more instance, the relief of pensioners. I submit, with all due respect to him, that .that is almost too puerile to mention in connection with a measure of this kind. The relief of pensioners, as my right hon. friend knows, is the subject from time to time of governor general's warrants because it is difficult to know just how much money as wanted. Further I would point out that even this year my right hon. friend who was not going to have any supplementary estimates at ali from last year, who was going to see that the departments kept within their appropriations, laid on the table supplementary estimates amounting to something like $700,000 for the relief of pensioners. What has that to do with the measure with which we are dealing to-day? Nothing whatever, but mentioning all these irrelevant things helps to make people feel that the Prime Minister must have a vast store of information and gives them the impression that he must know what he is talking about. Many references are put on the record and people feel that they must foe arguments or the Prime Minister would not make them. They do not know him as we do. He often makes the worse appear the better reason. He substitutes information for argument, information which while very interesting does not contribute much in support of the particular thesis he is presenting at the time.

The bill originally was
for March 31; the right hon. gentleman opposite admitted that to have the bill run to March 31 at a time when parliament was sitting would be a usurpation of powers, and therefore he limited it to March 1. What was the situation? The situation was that last year parliament met on March 12. I have no doubt my right hon. friend expected that this year it would meet about the same day, and he was content that the date of expiry of the bill should be coincident with the meeting of parliament. He indicated plainly that if this bill were in force this year while parliament was sitting there would be a usurpation of the people's rights.
In the light of what is now proposed I should like again to read from the statement made last year by the right hon. gentleman:
I will shorten the time to March 1 and make it clear that we have no desire to usurp powers as was suggested.
Now what does he purpose doing? I shall paraphrase his words, "I will lengthen the time to May 1 and make it clear that we do desire to usurp the powers, as was suggested." This is the right hon. gentleman who brushes to one side a constitutional question and says there is nothing in it, but who last year promised this parliament and country that after March 1, 1932, that monstrosity passed last year would not be upon the statute books.
My right hon. friend has given a number of instances in which he says extraordinary powers might be useful. There have been pointed out time and again the possibility of the extraordinary use of such powers, uses which would be quite within the letter and the spirit of the statute. Instances were given the other night. Let me remind the house that, if this bill becomes law, until May 1, with parliament sitting, my right hon. friend and his government if they liked could disfranchise any member who dared to criticize the government. Sitting over in the east block he could pass an amendment to the elections act. He has already amended the Insurance Act and he could amend any other statute. He has probably looked into this aspect of the matter or he would not have come here at all; but I am not so sure that if he had taken time by the forelock, if he had thought of it in time, he might not have succeeded in perpetuating himself by amending and extending the act by order in council before it had expired. Evidently he did not want to take that chance. He came here on February 26 and asked for what he calls a renewal of the act, but it is not a renewal.

He speaks of a continuance of the act, but as we have pointed out to him, there is going to be a definite break between March 1, when the act expired, and the date when the new act is assented to, and my right hon. friend will not have any legalization for what has been done in the meantime.
I am trying to dig out all the reasons I can which have been given as to why this particular bill should become law. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) said that they needed the machinery provided under this bill; he says that this machinery is necessary, because there would be less disturbance if it were kept in operation. Let me ask: Is there any machinery in the world that would be changed in connection with the expenditure of the money whether it were spent under an ordinary parliamentary vote or under this statute. There is a director of employment, and he would still spend the money if it were voted under a supply bill founded upon estimates, just the same as he would spend it under this act. There are still subdirectors of employment in the different provinces; there is still the Department of Labour; exactly the same machinery would be used in either case, and the same kind of dollars would be paid out. I am afraid that in some cases the same sort of men would be employed in connection with the work, but I am sure there would be no change nor would there be any dislocation because of the fact that the money did not happen to be voted under this act but under an estimate passed by committee of the whole house and subsequently included in a supply bill. The only machinery wanting under the old act is provision for a director of peace, order and good government, and I think my right hon. friend will probably take care of that office himself. There is no need of any more machinery; there is no fear of dislocation of any kind or description. Canadian dollars are Canadian dollars no matter how they may be voted, but my right hon. friends demand that these Canadian dollars be accompanied by a complete surrender of all the rights of parliament and of the people.
I have spoken of the delay which has taken place, and in the moment or two left me I want to point out the situation in which my hon. friends opposite find themselves to-day. As a result of an absolute, callous indifference to this question of unemployment, as a result of the way in which hon. gentlemen opposite have treated it since the election this is the situation. The act has expired. A resolution was put on the order paper on February 26 but was never touched or mentioned by the

Unemployment Continuance Act
Prime Minister until March 8, and the debate has been going on since that time; and the position in which my right hon. friend finds himself to-day is that he had to have his Minister of Agriculture move yesterday that the question be now put. And this afternoon the right hon. gentleman has himself put on the gag by giving notice of closure on Tuesday next. What is the situation so far as supply is concerned? To the motion to go into supply an amendment has been moved by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Heenan), the former Minister of Labour, which motion has not yet been disposed of. Going into supply automatically is blocked for this reason, that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) has given the house an undertaking that the government will not proceed with any supply involving the ten per cent cut in civil service salaries, and the only estimates that are left to be considered are estimates of that kind. My right hon. friend will therefore find it necessary to dispose of the debate on deductions or reductions in civil service salaries before he can proceed with supply. And this jam, the position in which my hon. friends opposite find themselves now, is due simply to the delay and the indifference which they have manifested in connection with unemployment from the first of the session, when the matter should have been introduced and dealt with. Moreover, as my right hon. leader (Mr. Mackenzie King) points out, the financial year ends on March 31 next, so that probably the government will be coming to us for interim supply, because the voting of supply has been blocked by their own neglect and delay. Now that is a nice situation in which we are to break up as we go home for Easter.
I suppose my right hon. friend will not take any personal assurance from me, but I wish to give him one, and I believe I can get support for it if he still wants money for the relief of unemployment in Saskatchewan. And, by the way, I take the position that Saskatchewan is not the only province that needs unemployment relief. The people of my constituency and my province are in need of relief also. The fishermen there are in sore straits and need relief in the worst way. The only thing they have got so far is an extra lobster season to give them the great privilege, bless your heart, of six weeks' lobster fishing in the bleak months of December and January. That has been the extent of the unemployment relief they have obtained, with the addition of small works in connection with breakwaters and things of that kind. No real attempt has been made to
assist the fishermen. Now my assurance to my right hon. friend is that we will stay here this evening and pass-
And it is now five minutes to six o'clock.
I am suggesting-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Talk a little sense anyway.

I am suggesting to my
right hon. friend in all seriousness that we are quite willing to stay, but he does not want money to relieve unemployment; he wants power. Unless chapter 58 is handed over to my hon. friends opposite they will not take the money to relieve unemployment. That is the position. My right hon. friend must admit that there is no need of chapter 58 in the next six weeks. As a matter of fact, there is very little in chapter 58 which he required in the last year. But it has been a good thing for him to have in his hands, as he himself says-a weapon; that was the word he used. But, Mr. Speaker, we are still living, at least we thought we were living, in a democratic country, whose people send their representatives to parliament to take part in the discussion of all legislation. But, from what has been taking place, I do not know what the Prime Minister wants parliament for. I do not see why if we should reenact chapter 58 there is really any need of the House of Commons. He can sit over in the east block and do everything that parliament could do. Why bother with parliament at all? I am going to repeat the suggestion to the Prime Minister, nevertheless.

We can come back at
eight o'clock.

If the Prime Minister
wants money for unemployment relief in Saskatchewan, he can have it, and we will stay here until he gets it. Once more, however, he laughs; once more he receives the suggestion with levity. Let me tell him, however, that I am as serious in this suggestion as I can possibly be. If my right hon. friend would open his heart and tell us exactly what he thinks, I am sure that he is as sick as anyone that he ever thought of asking for chapter 58.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: He certainly is not.

He knows that chapter 58 is no good; his supporters have told him it is no good. I have no doubt .that in the caucus [DOT]held this morning they told him pretty freely

and plainly that they thought he was making a mistake in hanging on to chapter 58, but apparently he is going to do so.
Now, Mr. Speaker, just this last word: My right hon. friend, I take it from the way in which he received my suggestion, is not going to stay to-night and is not going to take the money from us. He is going to let the unemployed wait until after Easter, until the dragooning process is put through and parliament is forced to vote this money in his way and in no other.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Did I understand my hon. friend to say, " Take the money from us?"
Yes, that is right, from parliament. We are parliament.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The minority is going to hand out the money?

We are parliament, and
that minority argument does not carry my right hon. friend very far. Every hon. member here is a part of this House of Commons, and every man has an equal right to participate. While my right hon. friend's reference [DOT]to the government as a committee of this house may be correct in point of fact, really the government are advisers of the representative of the crown, who happen to be members of this house. The right hon. gentleman has admitted that my right hon. leader was right when a year ago and at the special session as well he suggested conferences. My [DOT]right hon. friend intimates that clandestinely, or apparently not openly, he has had some of *these conferences with the provincial premiers, one at a time. I suggest to him that in spite of the twenty hours a day he and his government are working, no more proper thing could be done during the Easter recess than to have a conference called here at Ottawa. We might even adjourn for a day or two longer in order that the Prime Minister might have the benefit of the combined brains and business judgment of people of various walks of life who know something about unemployment relief, who know what conditions are in different parts of the country, who are nonpartisan and who are actuated by only one [DOT]motive, and that is to relieve distress. I believe if he does that it will be possible to bring in a measure which will really implement the promises which he made.
I say this bill does not and has not, in the experience we have had with it, in any way met -the promises made by the Prime Minister. It has been ineffectual; it has been inadequate; it has been expensive; it has been extravagant. I want to repeat what cannot be repeated too often, that the money
rMr. Ralston.]
can be made available in the shortest possible time for the relief of unemployment if the Prime Minister really wants to relieve distress. I say, however, that as far as this side of the [DOT]house is concerned, we do not propose to surrender the right of the' people to control expenditure and taxation, which is one of the bulwarks of British institutions. We are not going to hand over the fortress of responsible government without a struggle and we refuse to be a party to this enactment unless by force of the gag invoked by a ruthless parliamentary majority. I tell my right hon. friend that he has forgotten the unemployed altogether in his avarice for power. I believe my right hon. friend would gladly retrace his steps if he had those steps to take over again, because he is coming to realize that his very success in forcing this measure through will be his defeat.

At six o'clock the house adjourned without question put, pursuant to standing order, until Tuesday, March 29, at three o'clock in the afternoon.
